records.sourceFile: Salivary biomarkers of tactical athlete readiness - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Lindsey B, Shaul Y, Martin J. Salivary biomarkers of tactical athlete readiness: A systematic review. PLoS One. 2025;20(4):e0321223.
paper.abstract: PRISMA systematic review of 49 studies of salivary biomarkers measured before and after sleep loss, dehydration, environmental and muscular-fatigue stressors in tactical athletes and healthy adults.
paper.tldr: Saliva can capture stress responses in the field, but cortisol and testosterone are inconsistent readiness markers. Proteomic and non-hormonal markers look more promising but are not yet practical for field use.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided review of PubMed, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus and Google Scholar, searched in early 2024, with duplicate screening, independent data extraction and Downs and Black quality ratings. Studies were grouped by stressor and biomarker and synthesised qualitatively without a pooled analysis.
paper.findings: Of 49 studies, 27 were rated good and 22 fair. Hormonal markers were most studied, and cortisol changes were mixed across stressors. In the five dehydration studies, osmolality and total protein rose and flow rate fell, while proteomic and metabolomic panels discriminated fatigue at 83% and 96% accuracy in single small studies.
paper.limitations: The authors report heterogeneity in methods, populations and assays, few power analyses, underrepresentation of women, and mostly quasi-experimental designs with a single post-stressor measure.
paper.practicalImplications: Saliva osmolality, total protein and flow rate were the most consistent hydration signals, though from only five dehydration studies, so they are the best-supported field candidates for now. Cortisol and testosterone need baseline and diurnal control before they can support readiness decisions.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Salivary hydration markers may help monitor hydration around training. The review found no consistent link between cortisol or testosterone and performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The review covers stress and readiness rather than injury recovery, so it cannot inform return to sport. Muscle-damage markers such as creatine kinase were studied after exercise, but sampling timelines varied and no study tested them for return decisions.

records.sourceFile: Scoping review of methods of monitoring acute changes in lower body neuromuscular function via force plates.pdf

paper.citation: Badby AJ, Ripley NJ, McMahon JJ, Mundy PD, Comfort P. Scoping review of methods of monitoring acute changes in lower body neuromuscular function via force plates. PLoS One. 2025;20(5):e0322820.
paper.abstract: A scoping review of 30 within-group repeated-measures studies that used force plates to monitor acute changes in lower-body neuromuscular function. The studies differed widely in participants, test selection, data collection, metric definitions and phase terminology. The authors conclude that generalized conclusions about specific tests and metrics are premature until standardized methods are used and reported.
paper.tldr: Force-plate monitoring studies differ widely in tests, metric definitions and protocols, so their results cannot yet be compared or combined. Jump height was the most used metric, and the authors call for the reliability and sensitivity of common metrics to be established before practical conclusions are drawn.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with searches of PubMed, EBSCO, Web of Science and Ovid to 24 June 2024. Inclusion covered English-language peer-reviewed studies of athletes, physically demanding occupations, students and recreational athletes that used force plates to assess acute (under one week) changes in lower-body neuromuscular function. Reference lists of eligible studies were screened, and 30 studies were included. Data on demographics, protocols, hardware, tests, metrics and time points were charted qualitatively.
paper.findings: Of the 30 studies, 466 participants were included. Countermovement jump was used in 23 studies, and 90 CMJ metrics were reported, with jump height the most common (14 studies). Peak force was calculated in different ways across studies, and braking, eccentric, propulsive and concentric phases were used inconsistently. Only 2 studies tracked body mass change, plate zeroing and body-weighing were each reported in only 6 studies, and 1000 Hz was the most common sampling rate (17 studies). After immediately post-activity testing, the most common time points were 24 h, 48 h and 72 h.
paper.limitations: The review is qualitative and descriptive with no quality appraisal, and no protocol was pre-registered. Six studies lacked enough results to be tabulated. The sample was predominantly male, with only 5 studies including females; the Discussion gives different sex counts (19 male and 3 female studies, 319 participants) than the Results (26 and 5 studies, 466 participants), apparently from the 24 tabulated studies. The review did not evaluate the reliability or sensitivity of the metrics it describes.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners using force plates to monitor acute change should fix and report the test protocol, including verbal cues, familiarization, surface, plate zeroing and body-weighing. They should also use several metric types (outcome, strategy, kinetic and ratio) rather than jump height alone, and check how their software defines peak force and phases before comparing with published values.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the review supports a standard countermovement jump protocol with consistent cues, zeroing and body-weighing, and tracking several metrics such as jump height, phase timing and force, with body mass alongside. Metric definitions differ across published work, so local software definitions should be checked before comparing with external benchmarks.
paper.rtp: The review does not inform return-to-sport decisions. It excluded studies focused on rehabilitation progression and concussion recovery, so it cannot support using these metrics to judge readiness after injury.

records.sourceFile: Serial ultrasonography for the assessment of healing of lower extremity bone stress injury and correlation with return to sport.pdf

paper.citation: Toresdahl BG, Conway J, Miller TT, Goolsby MA, Geannette CS, Quijano B, et al. Serial Ultrasonography for the Assessment of Healing of Lower Extremity Bone Stress Injury and Correlation With Return to Sport/Exercise. Sports Health. 2024.
paper.abstract: Prospective observational cohort of adults aged 18 to 50 with an MRI-confirmed exercise-related bone stress injury of the distal tibia, fibula or metatarsals. Serial ultrasound every two weeks for 12 weeks was correlated with pain (NRS) and return-to-sport ratings. Soft tissue edema and hyperemia decreased over time; hyperemia correlated with pain at weeks 4 and 6 and with return to sport at week 6.
paper.tldr: Ultrasound of lower-leg and foot stress injuries showed edema and hyperemia fading over 12 weeks, and hyperemia tracked pain and return-to-sport ratings around weeks 4 to 6. The correlations are weak and the study is small, so ultrasound looks promising for monitoring but is not a return-to-sport test yet.
paper.methods: Adults aged 18 to 50 with a recent exercise-related distal tibia, fibula or metatarsal bone stress injury confirmed by MRI were enrolled within four weeks of MRI and scanned every two weeks for 12 weeks. Two blinded musculoskeletal radiologists scored soft tissue edema, periosteal reaction, hyperemia (0 to 3) and callus. Patients completed pain (NRS) and return-to-sport surveys biweekly, and MRI was repeated at 12 weeks. Repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t tests and Spearman correlations were used.
paper.findings: Of 31 enrolled, 30 were analysed. Soft tissue edema, periosteal reaction and hyperemia were seen on ultrasound at some point in 66.7%, 63.3% and 43.3% of patients. Soft tissue edema fell from 0.95 at week 2 to 0.34 at week 12 and hyperemia from 0.63 to 0.07 (both P < .01); periosteal reaction did not change significantly in Table 3 (P = .23). Hyperemia correlated with average pain at week 4 (rho 0.45, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.69) and week 6 (rho 0.42, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.67), and with return to sport at week 6 (rho -0.45, 95% CI -0.68 to -0.09); patients with hyperemia at week 6 had higher pain in later weeks (P = .04) but not clearly lower return-to-sport ratings (P = .06). Soft tissue edema correlated with pain at week 6 (rho 0.38). MRI marrow edema fell from 1.3 to 0.79 (P < .01), but it persisted in 53.3% at 12 weeks and did not correlate with pain or return to sport.
paper.limitations: Single centre, no comparison group, small sample, and a 4-point subjective ultrasound scale with inter-observer variability. The return-to-sport scale was not validated, most patients had not fully returned by week 12, and no ultrasound correlations with clinical outcomes were significant after week 6. The Results text says periosteal reaction decreased significantly (all P < .01), but Table 3 gives P = .23; the abstract says 30 patients were enrolled, but the Results say 31 were enrolled and one was excluded after week 2; and Table 1 gives metatarsal 49.7% while the text gives 46.7%.
paper.practicalImplications: Ultrasound every two weeks could track hyperemia and soft tissue edema alongside symptoms, which may help where repeat MRI is less useful. The authors note athletic training rooms may be able to use it, but the findings support clinical judgment rather than replacing it.
paper.athleteDev: Not a performance application. Staff who manage progression after a bone stress injury could look at the trend in hyperemia and symptoms, but the study does not test load or training decisions.
paper.rtp: Hyperemia at week 6 was associated with lower return-to-sport ratings, so it may be a useful added signal. The paper cannot set a clearance threshold: correlations were weak, the return-to-sport scale was not validated, and no prognostic cut-off was derived.

records.sourceFile: Serum myokines as potential biomarkers of myostatin inhibition in sport doping - A preliminary study on their baseline levels in elite athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Donati F, Biasini GM, de la Torre X, Botrè F. Serum myokines as potential biomarkers of myostatin inhibition in sport doping: a preliminary study on their baseline levels in elite athletes. Biology of Sport. 2024;41(2):175-183.
paper.abstract: The authors measured serum myostatin and nine related myokines in elite athletes whose doping control samples were negative, to assess whether these markers could indicate myostatin inhibition. Concentrations varied by several orders of magnitude, females had higher FSTL-1 and musclin, and power athletes had higher IGF-1 and BDNF than endurance athletes. Musclin, FSTL-1 and oncostatin clustered most closely with myostatin.
paper.tldr: Baseline serum levels of myostatin and related myokines were measured in 53 negative-testing elite athletes. The panel is a starting point for reference ranges, not a validated doping test.
paper.methods: Serum from routine doping control samples from elite athletes (myostatin n=53; 41 males, 12 females; mean age 26.6 years) was assayed by ELISA, radioimmunoassay and multiplex bead array. Groups were compared with Mann-Whitney U tests, correlations were Kendall's tau-beta, and a principal component analysis was run on a paired subset (N=41).
paper.findings: Myokine concentrations ranged from under 1 ng/mL (musclin, osteonectin) to above 10 ng/mL (BDNF, FSTL-1, IGF-1). FSTL-1 and musclin were higher in females (p<0.05), and IGF-1 and BDNF were higher in power than endurance athletes (p=0.006 and p=0.001). Myostatin correlated with oncostatin (tau 0.23, p<0.05); the text also describes a significant correlation with FSTL-1, but Table 3 gives 0.17 for that pair without a significance mark. The FOL/MYO ratio was below 1 and varied widely (mean 0.34, CV 64%).
paper.limitations: The female subgroups are small (n=6 to 13 depending on the analyte), so sex differences may be unreliable, and the authors note this as a likely confounder. The samples come from athletes with negative routine doping control results, and the paper does not test any myostatin inhibitor or report intra-individual change over time. The text and Table 3 disagree on whether the myostatin-FSTL-1 correlation is significant. Abstract and results agree on the sex and sport comparisons.
paper.practicalImplications: Anti-doping and research staff can use these values as a first reference for clean elite athletes, but a single sample cannot identify myostatin inhibition. The authors suggest that any future use would need repeated sampling within each athlete.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not give training or performance recommendations. Its value to performance staff is limited to knowing that IGF-1 and BDNF differed between power and endurance athletes in this sample.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It measured baseline serum markers in athletes with negative doping control results and says nothing about injury, healing or recovery after injury.

records.sourceFile: Sleep Monitoring in Athletes- Motivation, Methods, Miscalculations and Why it Matters.pdf

paper.citation: Halson SL. Sleep Monitoring in Athletes: Motivation, Methods, Miscalculations and Why it Matters. Sports Med. 2019.
paper.abstract: This review outlines reasons for sleep disturbance in athletes, the advantages and disadvantages of methods to assess sleep (polysomnography, activity monitoring, consumer sleep technology, sleep diaries and questionnaires), considerations for feedback, and intervention and behaviour change strategies. It is written to give practitioners current evidence in an area where monitoring is growing faster than standards.
paper.tldr: Athlete sleep monitoring needs validated tools, careful interpretation and supportive feedback. Research-grade actigraphy with a sleep diary is the most defensible option in this review, while consumer wearables and apps are better used to start conversations than to make decisions.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the literature on sleep assessment in athletes. It describes each monitoring tool with its advantages and disadvantages, a suggested monitoring process, and a worked case of one Olympic athlete monitored with a 14-day actigraphy and diary period.
paper.findings: Research-grade activity monitors agreed with polysomnography in athletes (81 to 90% agreement, 81 to 92% sensitivity), but their accuracy depends on the scoring threshold. In one study of 12 semi-professional soccer players, a consumer wearable's mean total sleep time difference from polysomnography was 51.5 min (SD 152.4) with very wide limits, and a popular sleep app showed no correlation with polysomnography for sleep efficiency. In one rugby league study, education and monitoring improved sleep only during the education period.
paper.limitations: The review has no described systematic search, and its conclusions rest partly on small validation studies. The author notes that there are currently no published validation studies of some popular wearables, and that there are no standard monitoring procedures or guidelines for athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: A practical approach is a 1 to 2 week actigraphy period with a sleep diary during a training cycle, with referral to a sleep physician if a sleep disorder is suspected. Consumer device and app data should be used as a starting point for discussion, and feedback should focus on what can be improved rather than on poor scores.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff could use a 14-day actigraphy and diary period during a training block to find routine problems such as inconsistent bed and wake times, as the case study does. Feedback should focus on the aspects that can be changed, and wearable sleep scores should not drive training decisions until they are validated.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return-to-sport timing or injured athletes. Its only point relevant to rehabilitation staff is that a suspected sleep disorder should be investigated and referred to a sleep physician as a priority.
